name: Fungal skin infections
tagline: Athlete's foot, ringworm, jock itch. Cheap to treat.

what_is_it.heading: Fungal skin infections in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Fungal skin infections are caused by tiny harmless fungi that live on warm, moist parts of the body. When they overgrow, they cause itchy, scaly, often ring-shaped patches. Annoying but generally easy to treat.
paragraphs: Common types: athlete's foot (between toes), jock itch (groin), ringworm (anywhere — actually a fungus, not a worm), nail fungus, scalp ringworm in children. Despite different names, they're all caused by similar fungi.

Most respond to over-the-counter antifungal cream applied for 2–4 weeks. Some — nail fungus, scalp infections — need prescription tablets. People with diabetes, weakened immune systems, or HIV may get more severe or recurring infections.

items.headline: Very common
items.body: Athlete's foot alone affects up to 70% of adults at some point. Ringworm and jock itch are common worldwide.

items.headline: Easy to treat
items.body: Most fungal skin infections clear with over-the-counter cream in 2–4 weeks. Cheap, available at any pharmacy.

items.headline: Contagious
items.body: Fungus spreads on towels, shower floors, gym mats, shared shoes. Treat it — and don't share towels or footwear during treatment.

items.headline: Keep dry
items.body: Fungus loves warm, moist skin. Dry thoroughly after bathing, change sweaty socks and underwear, air out shoes. Prevention is mostly about dryness.

pull_quote.text: If a 'ring' on the skin doesn't clear with antifungal cream in 4 weeks, see a doctor. Some other skin conditions look like ringworm — and steroid cream will make a real ringworm worse.

signs.heading: Common patterns
signs.lede: Fungal infections all share an itchy, scaly, often ring-shaped look — but where they show up varies.

items.title: Athlete's foot
items.description: Itchy, cracking, peeling skin between toes — especially the 4th and 5th. Can spread to soles. Smells. Worsens in summer and with sweaty shoes.

items.title: Ringworm (tinea corporis)
items.description: Round red (or darker, on Black skin) scaly patch with a clear centre — looks like a ring. Slowly grows outwards. Common on arms, neck, body. Itchy.

items.title: Jock itch and scalp tinea
items.description: Jock itch: red, itchy rash in the groin folds — common in men, after sweating. Scalp ringworm: patchy hair loss with scaling — common in children, needs tablets.

spreads.heading: How fungal infections spread
yes: Direct skin-to-skin contact with an infected person
Shared towels, bed linen, clothing, hairbrushes
Walking barefoot on contaminated floors — public showers, gym changing rooms, swimming pool decks
From pets (cats and dogs can carry ringworm)
From sweaty equipment in gyms or sport
no: Casual contact like shaking hands or hugging

prevention.heading: How to avoid getting it again
prevention.lede: Fungus comes back if conditions remain warm and moist. Small daily habits prevent most recurrences.

items.title: Dry thoroughly after washing
items.description: Especially between toes, in groin, under breasts, in skin folds. Pat dry. A dry skin is an unfriendly home for fungus.

items.title: Clean cotton, change often
items.description: Cotton socks and underwear breathe better than synthetics. Change daily and after sweating. Don't re-wear sweaty gym clothes.

items.title: Don't go barefoot in public
items.description: Public showers, gym changing rooms, swimming pool decks — wear slops or sandals. Most fungal foot infections come from these places.

items.title: Don't share towels or shoes
items.description: Even with family members. If someone has a fungal infection, use separate towels until it has cleared.

items.title: Start over-the-counter antifungal cream
items.description: Clotrimazole or terbinafine — apply twice a day to the affected area plus 2cm around it. Keep going for 2 weeks after the rash clears to prevent return.

items.title: Keep the area dry and exposed to air
items.description: Don't bandage. Wear loose clothing. Let the skin breathe. Powder (not cream) in the morning can help in groin or feet for sweat absorption.

items.title: Treat the source
items.description: Wash all towels, bedding, and clothes that touched the infection in hot water. Throw out or disinfect old shoes if athlete's foot keeps coming back.

items.title: If not better in 4 weeks — see a doctor
items.description: Some look-alike conditions don't respond to antifungal. Nail fungus and scalp ringworm need tablets. Government clinics provide both free.

items.title: If you have diabetes or HIV — go early
items.description: Fungal infections can be more severe and spread faster. Go to clinic at the first sign — don't wait to try over-the-counter for weeks.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Most fungal skin infections clear with cheap over-the-counter cream. If they don't, government clinics provide free prescription treatment.

helplines.name: Find your nearest clinic
helplines.description: Free assessment and prescription antifungal treatment if needed
helplines.meta: No appointment · no medical aid required
